claim: Cholesterol partitions into accessible and sequestered pools in cell membranes.
source: Cholesterol partitions into accessible and sequestered pools in cell membranes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cholesterol behavior in membranes.

claim: A new assay using fluorescently-tagged anthrolysin O measures accessible cholesterol in human red blood cells (RBCs).
source: Here, we describe a new assay using fluorescently-tagged anthrolysin O, a cholesterol-binding bacterial toxin, to measure accessible cholesterol in human red blood cells (RBCs).
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and validation of this assay throughout the Results section.

claim: Accessible cholesterol levels were stable within individuals.
source: Accessible cholesterol levels were stable within individuals, but varied >10 fold among individuals.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3B showing measurements over time in five individuals.

claim: Accessible cholesterol levels varied more than 10 fold among individuals.
source: Accessible cholesterol levels were stable within individuals, but varied >10 fold among individuals.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3A and Figure 5 showing distribution across 364 individuals.

claim: Significant variation in accessible cholesterol was observed among ethnic groups with the pattern Blacks>Hispanics>Whites.
source: Significant variation was observed among ethnic groups (Blacks>Hispanics>Whites).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 5 and Table 2 showing median values and statistical significance.

claim: Variation in accessibility of RBC cholesterol was unrelated to the cholesterol content of RBCs.
source: Variation in accessibility of RBC cholesterol was unrelated to the cholesterol content of RBCs or plasma, but was associated with the phospholipid composition of the RBC membranes and with plasma triglyceride levels.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4C showing no correlation between cholesterol content and fALOD4 binding.

claim: Variation in accessibility of RBC cholesterol was unrelated to plasma cholesterol content.
source: Variation in accessibility of RBC cholesterol was unrelated to the cholesterol content of RBCs or plasma, but was associated with the phospholipid composition of the RBC membranes and with plasma triglyceride levels.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7 showing no significant correlation with plasma total cholesterol.

claim: Variation in accessibility of RBC cholesterol was associated with the phospholipid composition of the RBC membranes.
source: Variation in accessibility of RBC cholesterol was unrelated to the cholesterol content of RBCs or plasma, but was associated with the phospholipid composition of the RBC membranes and with plasma triglyceride levels.
evidence: Supported by data in Table 4 and Table 5 showing associations with LPE, SM, and PA.

claim: Variation in accessibility of RBC cholesterol was associated with plasma triglyceride levels.
source: Variation in accessibility of RBC cholesterol was unrelated to the cholesterol content of RBCs or plasma, but was associated with the phospholipid composition of the RBC membranes and with plasma triglyceride levels.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7 and Table 2 showing inverse correlation with plasma TG.

claim: Pronase treatment of RBCs only modestly altered cholesterol accessibility.
source: Pronase treatment of RBCs only modestly altered cholesterol accessibility.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 8A showing ~25% increase at lowest pronase concentration.

claim: Individuals on hemodialysis had significantly higher RBC cholesterol accessibility.
source: Individuals on hemodialysis, who have an unexplained increase in atherosclerotic risk, had significantly higher RBC cholesterol accessibility.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 10A comparing dialysis patients to controls.

claim: Individuals on hemodialysis have an unexplained increase in atherosclerotic risk.
source: Individuals on hemodialysis, who have an unexplained increase in atherosclerotic risk, had significantly higher RBC cholesterol accessibility.
evidence: This is cited knowledge referenced in the manuscript (Levey et al., 1998).

claim: RBC accessible cholesterol is a stable phenotype with significant inter-individual variability.
source: Our data indicate that RBC accessible cholesterol is a stable phenotype with significant inter-individual variability.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3 showing stability within individuals and variation among individuals.

claim: Factors both intrinsic and extrinsic to the RBC contribute to variation in cholesterol accessibility.
source: Factors both intrinsic and extrinsic to the RBC contribute to variation in its accessibility.
evidence: Supported by data showing associations with RBC membrane lipids (intrinsic) and plasma TG (extrinsic).

claim: Cholesterol is an essential component of vertebrate cell membranes.
source: Cholesterol is an essential component of vertebrate cell membranes (Goldstein et al., 1979).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: All cells in the body except red blood cells (RBCs) synthesize cholesterol.
source: All cells in the body except red blood cells (RBCs) synthesize cholesterol.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RBC metabolism.

claim: The major pathway for cholesterol excretion in humans is via the biliary system.
source: The major pathway for cholesterol excretion in humans is via the biliary system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cholesterol metabolism.

claim: The proteins and processes by which cholesterol is secreted into the bile have been well characterized.
source: The proteins and processes by which cholesterol is secreted into the bile, either directly, or after conversion to bile acids, have been well characterized (Berge et al., 2000; Russell, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The process by which cholesterol from peripheral tissues is delivered to the liver for excretion remains poorly defined.
source: In contrast, the process by which cholesterol from peripheral tissues is delivered to the liver for excretion remains poorly defined.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A mechanism for the centripetal trafficking of cholesterol from extrahepatic tissues to the liver has been termed reverse cholesterol transport.
source: A mechanism for the centripetal trafficking of cholesterol from extrahepatic tissues to the liver, which has been termed reverse cholesterol transport, was first conceptualized by Glomset (1968).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Glomset (1968).

claim: High density lipoproteins (HDL) have been implicated as an essential component of reverse cholesterol transport.
source: That work, and subsequent studies, have implicated high density lipoproteins (HDL) as an essential component of this pathway (Bailey, 1964) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Free cholesterol is transferred from cells to HDL by ATP binding cassette, subfamily A, member 1 (ABCA1).
source: Free cholesterol is transferred from cells to HDL by ATP binding cassette, subfamily A, member 1 (ABCA1) (Lawn et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lawn et al., 1999.

claim: Free cholesterol in HDL is esterified with long-chain fatty acids by lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT).
source: The free cholesterol in the HDL particle is then esterified with long-chain fatty acids by lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) (Glomset, 1968) and sequestered in a hydrophobic core below the phospholipid surface of HDL (Stoffel et al., 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Glomset (1968) and Stoffel et al. (1974).

claim: Cholesteryl ester is sequestered in a hydrophobic core below the phospholipid surface of HDL.
source: The free cholesterol in the HDL particle is then esterified with long-chain fatty acids by lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) (Glomset, 1968) and sequestered in a hydrophobic core below the phospholipid surface of HDL (Stoffel et al., 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stoffel et al. (1974).

claim: Sequestration of cholesterol in the HDL core decreases the propensity of cholesterol to exchange with cell membranes.
source: This step is critical to the delivery of cholesterol to the liver; sequestration in the HDL core decreases the propensity of cholesterol to exchange with cell membranes, thus limiting the retrograde transfer of cholesterol from HDL back to the tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biophysical properties of cholesterol esters.

claim: Cholesteryl ester is delivered to the liver directly via scavenger receptor class B member 1 (SCARB1).
source: The cholesteryl ester is then delivered to the liver either directly via a cell surface receptor, scavenger receptor class B member 1 (SCARB1) (Acton et al., 1996), or indirectly after transferring the cholesterol to Apolipoprotein (Apo)B-containing lipoproteins, which then undergo endocytosis by the low density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Acton et al. (1996) and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Cholesteryl ester is delivered to the liver indirectly after transferring to ApoB-containing lipoproteins, which undergo endocytosis by the LDLR.
source: The cholesteryl ester is then delivered to the liver either directly via a cell surface receptor, scavenger receptor class B member 1 (SCARB1) (Acton et al., 1996), or indirectly after transferring the cholesterol to Apolipoprotein (Apo)B-containing lipoproteins, which then undergo endocytosis by the low density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about lipoprotein metabolism illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Several components of the HDL-mediated reverse cholesterol transport pathway have been supported by studies in cultured cells and in vivo.
source: Several components of the HDL-mediated reverse cholesterol transport pathway have been supported by studies in cultured cells and in vivo (Lewis and Rader, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lewis and Rader (2005).

claim: Mice lacking ABCA1 or ApoA1 have very low HDL levels.
source: Mice lacking ABCA1, or ApoA1, the major structural protein of HDL, have very low HDL levels and yet have no alterations in cholesterol turnover in peripheral tissues (Xie et al., 2009; Jolley et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xie et al. (2009) and Jolley et al. (1998).

claim: Mice lacking ABCA1 or ApoA1 have no alterations in cholesterol turnover in peripheral tissues.
source: Mice lacking ABCA1, or ApoA1, the major structural protein of HDL, have very low HDL levels and yet have no alterations in cholesterol turnover in peripheral tissues (Xie et al., 2009; Jolley et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xie et al. (2009) and Jolley et al. (1998).

claim: Glomset proposed that RBCs may participate in the transport of cholesterol from tissues to the liver.
source: Glomset proposed that RBCs may participate in the transport of cholesterol from tissues to the liver (Glomset, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Glomset (1968).

claim: Approximately 50% of circulating cholesterol is carried in RBC membranes.
source: Approximately 50% of circulating cholesterol is carried in RBC membranes and tracer studies in humans indicate that the magnitude of the cholesterol flux through RBCs is comparable to the total efflux of free cholesterol from tissues (Turner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Turner et al. (2012).

claim: The magnitude of cholesterol flux through RBCs is comparable to the total efflux of free cholesterol from tissues.
source: Approximately 50% of circulating cholesterol is carried in RBC membranes and tracer studies in humans indicate that the magnitude of the cholesterol flux through RBCs is comparable to the total efflux of free cholesterol from tissues (Turner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Turner et al. (2012).

claim: Cholesterol exchanges freely between RBCs, plasma, circulating lipoproteins, and cells.
source: Cholesterol exchanges freely between RBCs, plasma, circulating lipoproteins, and cells (Hagerman and Gould, 1951) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hagerman and Gould (1951) and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Reducing the number of RBCs in ApoA1 knockout mice decreases the transfer of radiolabeled cholesterol from macrophages to feces.
source: More recently, Smith and colleagues (Hung et al., 2012) showed that reducing the number of RBCs in ApoA1 knockout mice, which have little to no circulating HDL, decreases the transfer of radiolabeled cholesterol from macrophages to feces.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hung et al. (2012).

claim: For RBCs to participate in reverse cholesterol transport, the cholesterol must be located in the outer leaflet of the RBC membrane.
source: For RBCs to participate in reverse cholesterol transport, the cholesterol must be located in the outer leaflet of the RBC membrane, and thus accessible for transfer to proteins and cells.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of cholesterol transfer.

claim: The accessibility of cholesterol in a membrane is related to its chemical activity.
source: The accessibility of cholesterol in a membrane is related to its chemical activity (McConnell and Radhakrishnan, 2003), alternatively referred to as its fugacity (tendency to flee).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McConnell and Radhakrishnan (2003).

claim: The chemical activity of cholesterol generally increases with increasing cholesterol concentration.
source: The chemical activity of cholesterol generally increases with increasing cholesterol concentration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cholesterol biophysics.

claim: Complex formation with phospholipids can suppress the chemical activity of cholesterol below what would be expected in the absence of lipid interactions.
source: However, at lower concentrations, complex formation with phospholipids can suppress the chemical activity of cholesterol below what would be expected in the absence of lipid interactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cholesterol-phospholipid interactions.

claim: Sharp rises in chemical activity have been detected in model membranes by measurements of cholesterol accessibility using cyclodextrin extraction.
source: Sharp rises in chemical activity have been detected in model membranes by measurements of cholesterol accessibility, as assayed by cyclodextrin extraction (Radhakrishnan and McConnell, 2000; Litz et al., 2016), oxidation by cholesterol oxidase (Ahn and Sampson, 2004; Lange et al., 2013), and binding of cholesterol-dependent cytolysins such as perfringolysin O (PFO) or anthrolysin O (ALO) (Heuck et al., 2000; Gay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Radhakrishnan and McConnell (2000) and Litz et al. (2016).

claim: Sharp rises in chemical activity have been detected in model membranes by oxidation by cholesterol oxidase.
source: Sharp rises in chemical activity have been detected in model membranes by measurements of cholesterol accessibility, as assayed by cyclodextrin extraction (Radhakrishnan and McConnell, 2000; Litz et al., 2016), oxidation by cholesterol oxidase (Ahn and Sampson, 2004; Lange et al., 2013), and binding of cholesterol-dependent cytolysins such as perfringolysin O (PFO) or anthrolysin O (ALO) (Heuck et al., 2000; Gay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahn and Sampson (2004) and Lange et al. (2013).

claim: Sharp rises in chemical activity have been detected in model membranes by binding of cholesterol-dependent cytolysins such as perfringolysin O (PFO) or anthrolysin O (ALO).
source: Sharp rises in chemical activity have been detected in model membranes by measurements of cholesterol accessibility, as assayed by cyclodextrin extraction (Radhakrishnan and McConnell, 2000; Litz et al., 2016), oxidation by cholesterol oxidase (Ahn and Sampson, 2004; Lange et al., 2013), and binding of cholesterol-dependent cytolysins such as perfringolysin O (PFO) or anthrolysin O (ALO) (Heuck et al., 2000; Gay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heuck et al. (2000) and Gay et al. (2015).

claim: A sharp rise in the chemical activity of RBC membrane cholesterol has been observed using the cholesterol oxidase assay.
source: A sharp rise in the chemical activity of RBC membrane cholesterol has been observed using the cholesterol oxidase assay to assess cholesterol accessibility (Lange et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lange et al. (1980).

claim: The increase in cholesterol accessibility with increasing cholesterol concentration was sigmoidal, rather than linear.
source: In all of these cases, the increase in cholesterol accessibility with increasing cholesterol concentration was sigmoidal, rather than linear, with little change until a threshold concentration was reached.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from multiple cited studies and confirmed by data in Figure 2D.

claim: Once the cholesterol content of the membrane exceeded a threshold, accessibility of membrane cholesterol increased sharply.
source: Once the cholesterol content of the membrane exceeded this threshold, accessibility of membrane cholesterol increased sharply.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2D showing sigmoidal relationship.

claim: ALO is a cholesterol-binding toxin produced by Bacillus anthracis.
source: Using this assay, we show that RBC cholesterol accessibility is stable within individuals, but varies over a more than ten-fold range between individuals. To address the basis for the inter-individual variation in accessible RBC cholesterol, we examined the effect of demographic, physiologic, and biochemical differences among individuals on this newly described trait. Whereas age and gender had modest effects on accessible RBC cholesterol, significant ethnic differences were apparent in RBC cholesterol accessibility.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bourdeau et al. (2009) in the Introduction.

claim: A recombinant protein consisting of the cholesterol binding domain 4 (D4) of ALO was purified from E. coli and covalently modified with a maleimide-linked fluorescent dye (Alexa Fluor 488).
source: As described previously, a recombinant protein consisting of the cholesterol binding domain 4 (D4) of ALO was purified from E. coli and covalently modified with a maleimide-linked fluorescent dye (Alexa Fluor 488) (Gay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gay et al. (2015) and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: fALOD4 does not lyse RBCs.
source: This reagent, which does not lyse RBCs (Gay et al., 2015), is referred to hereafter as fALOD4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gay et al. (2015) and hemolysis data in Figure 2C.

claim: The extent of fALOD4 binding per cell increased with increasing concentrations of fALOD4.
source: The extent of fALOD4 binding per cell increased with increasing concentrations of fALOD4 (left panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C left panel.

claim: Even at the highest concentrations of fALOD4 tested, binding did not saturate.
source: Even at the highest concentrations of fALOD4 tested, binding did not saturate.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C left panel.

claim: At 250 nM fALOD4, binding approached saturation after 3 hr.
source: At this concentration, binding approached saturation after 3 hr, and this incubation time was chosen for subsequent assays.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C right panel.

claim: The assay conditions did not result in significant hemolysis (<5%).
source: These assay conditions did not result in significant hemolysis (<5%) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No fALOD4 binding was observed when the cholesterol content of the RBCs was reduced below ~46 mole%.
source: No fALOD4 binding was observed when the cholesterol content of the RBCs was reduced below ~46 mole%.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D left panel.

claim: Above the threshold of ~46 mole% cholesterol, fALOD4 binding increased sharply.
source: Above this apparent threshold, the binding increased sharply.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D left panel.

claim: When the data were plotted on a log-linear scale the relationship between cholesterol content of the membranes and fALOD4 binding was linear.
source: When the data were plotted on a log-linear scale the relationship between cholesterol content of the membranes and fALOD4 binding was linear (Figure 2D, inset, left panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D inset.

claim: A small reduction in cholesterol content of the cell was associated with a marked reduction in fALOD4 binding.
source: In cells incubated with increasing concentrations of HPCD, a small reduction in cholesterol content of the cell was associated with a marked reduction in fALOD4 binding (Figure 2D, right panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D right panel.

claim: Sigmoidal dependences on cholesterol concentration have been observed previously for the binding of cholesterol-binding toxins like ALO and PFO to model liposomes.
source: Such sigmoidal dependences on cholesterol concentration have been observed previously for the binding of cholesterol-binding toxins like ALO and PFO to model liposomes (thresholds vary from 20–50 mole% depending on the phospholipid content) (Gay et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2008), to plasma membranes (PM) of human fibroblasts (threshold ~35 mole%) (Das et al., 2013), and to purified ER membranes from cultured CHO-K1 cells (threshold ~5 mole%) (Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gay et al. (2015) and Nelson et al. (2008).

claim: Sigmoidal dependences on cholesterol concentration have been observed for binding of toxins to plasma membranes of human fibroblasts with threshold ~35 mole%.
source: Such sigmoidal dependences on cholesterol concentration have been observed previously for the binding of cholesterol-binding toxins like ALO and PFO to model liposomes (thresholds vary from 20–50 mole% depending on the phospholipid content) (Gay et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2008), to plasma membranes (PM) of human fibroblasts (threshold ~35 mole%) (Das et al., 2013), and to purified ER membranes from cultured CHO-K1 cells (threshold ~5 mole%) (Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Das et al. (2013).

claim: Sigmoidal dependences on cholesterol concentration have been observed for binding of toxins to purified ER membranes from cultured CHO-K1 cells with threshold ~5 mole%.
source: Such sigmoidal dependences on cholesterol concentration have been observed previously for the binding of cholesterol-binding toxins like ALO and PFO to model liposomes (thresholds vary from 20–50 mole% depending on the phospholipid content) (Gay et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2008), to plasma membranes (PM) of human fibroblasts (threshold ~35 mole%) (Das et al., 2013), and to purified ER membranes from cultured CHO-K1 cells (threshold ~5 mole%) (Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sokolov and Radhakrishnan (2010).

claim: fALOD4 binding varied over a 10-fold range among samples from different individuals.
source: fALOD4 binding varied over a 10-fold range (from 0.2 to 2.6) among samples from different individuals but the correlation between the two measurements on the same sample was very high (R = 0.94) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The correlation between duplicate measurements on the same sample was very high (R = 0.94).
source: fALOD4 binding varied over a 10-fold range (from 0.2 to 2.6) among samples from different individuals but the correlation between the two measurements on the same sample was very high (R = 0.94) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The intra-assay coefficient of variation for the assay was 10.7% ± 5.3%.
source: The intra-assay coefficient of variation for the assay was 10.7% ± 5.3%.
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Figure 3A.

claim: The intra-individual variation in fALOD4 binding per cell was 8.8% ± 4.2% (range: 3.6–12.8%).
source: The intra-individual variation in fALOD4 binding per cell was 8.8% ± 4.2% (range: 3.6–12.8%).
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Figure 3B.

claim: The inter-individual variation in fALOD4 binding per RBC was much greater than the variability seen in any given individual.
source: Thus, the inter-individual variation in fALOD4 binding per RBC was much greater than the variability seen in any given individual.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing data in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: No relationship was found between the cholesterol content of the RBC membranes and normalized fALOD4 binding.
source: Surprisingly, no relationship was found between the cholesterol content of the RBC membranes and normalized fALOD4 binding (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: fALOD4 binding does not simply reflect the cholesterol content of the RBC membrane.
source: Thus, fALOD4 binding does not simply reflect the cholesterol content of the RBC membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Accessible RBC cholesterol levels did not vary significantly with age.
source: Accessible RBC cholesterol levels did not vary significantly with age (Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2 with p=0.46.

claim: Men had significantly higher levels of accessible RBC cholesterol (p=0.01).
source: Men had significantly higher levels of accessible RBC cholesterol (p=0.01), although these differences were modest compared to the variation in levels among the three ethnic groups (Figure 5 and Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: The distribution of fALOD4 binding to RBCs was positively skewed and varied over a >10 fold range in all three ethnic groups.
source: In all three groups, the distribution of fALOD4 binding to RBCs was positively skewed and varied over a >10 fold range (Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: Median fALOD4 binding was lowest in Whites (0.77 nRFU), intermediate in Hispanics (0.86 nRFU), and highest in Blacks (1.18 nRFU) (p<0.0001).
source: Median fALOD4 binding was lowest in Whites (0.77 nRFU), intermediate in Hispanics (0.86 nRFU), and highest in Blacks (1.18 nRFU) (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and Table 2.

claim: No significant association was found between fALOD4 binding and RBC indices after adjustment for age, gender, and ethnicity.
source: No significant association was found between fALOD4 binding and RBC indices, including hematocrit, Hb concentration, RBC count, MCHC, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) or RBC distribution width (RDW), after adjustment for age, gender, and ethnicity (Table 1 and Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: The differences in RBC cholesterol accessibility levels among individuals or among the three different ethnicities did not appear to be related to differences in the gross morphology or Hb content of the RBC.
source: Thus, the differences in RBC cholesterol accessibility levels among individuals or among the three different ethnicities did not appear to be related to differences in the gross morphology or Hb content of the RBC.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of associations shown in Figure 6.

claim: fALOD4 binding to RBCs was not related significantly to plasma levels of total cholesterol, LDL-C or HDL-C levels.
source: fALOD4 binding to RBCs was not related significantly to plasma levels of total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C) or high-density lipoprotein (HDL)-C levels but was inversely related (p=0.0018) to plasma TG levels (Figure 7).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: fALOD4 binding to RBCs was inversely related (p=0.0018) to plasma TG levels.
source: fALOD4 binding to RBCs was not related significantly to plasma levels of total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C) or high-density lipoprotein (HDL)-C levels but was inversely related (p=0.0018) to plasma TG levels (Figure 7).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: Ethnicity accounted for 14.63% of the variance in fALOD4 binding.
source: The proportion of variance in fALOD4 binding that was explained by ethnicity in a model adjusted for age, sex, and plasma lipid levels was 14.63% (Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: Plasma TG (p=0.00021) and total cholesterol levels (p=0.026) contributed significantly to the variance of fALOD4 binding in a multivariable model adjusted for demographic factors.
source: Only plasma TG (p=0.00021) and total cholesterol levels (p=0.026) contributed significantly to the variance of fALOD4 binding in a multivariable model adjusted for demographic factors (Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: Age, gender, race, plasma TG and cholesterol levels accounted for 21.61% of the inter-individual variability in fALOD4 binding.
source: Together, age, gender, race, plasma TG and cholesterol levels accounted for 21.61% of the inter-individual variability in fALOD4 binding.
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: At the lowest concentration of pronase (0.02 μg/mL), fALOD4 binding increased by ~25%.
source: At the lowest concentration of pronase (0.02 μg/mL), fALOD4 binding increased by ~25% (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Higher concentrations of pronase did not further increase fALOD4 binding despite further decreases in membrane protein content.
source: Higher concentrations of pronase did not further increase fALOD4 binding despite further decreases in membrane protein content.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The protein composition of the RBC membrane is not a major determinant of fALOD4 binding.
source: Based on these results we concluded that the protein composition of the RBC membrane is not a major determinant of fALOD4 binding, although we cannot exclude the possibility that a protein(s) that is resistant to pronase treatment contributes to the inter-individual differences in fALOD4 binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the pronase treatment data in Figure 8A.

claim: No significant differences in fALOD4 binding were apparent between individuals with blood types A, B, and O.
source: No significant differences were apparent between individuals with blood types A, B, and O, whereas individuals who were Rhesus antigen negative (Rh-) had significantly lower fALOD4 binding than did individuals who were Rh+.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B upper panel.

claim: Individuals who were Rhesus antigen negative (Rh-) had significantly lower fALOD4 binding than did individuals who were Rh+.
source: No significant differences were apparent between individuals with blood types A, B, and O, whereas individuals who were Rhesus antigen negative (Rh-) had significantly lower fALOD4 binding than did individuals who were Rh+.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B lower panel.

claim: fALOD4 binding increased progressively when the RBCs were incubated with increasing amounts of PLA2.
source: fALOD4 binding increased progressively when the RBCs were incubated with increasing amounts of PLA2 (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Increased fALOD4 binding was seen after the cells were incubated with SMase.
source: Increased fALOD4 binding was also seen after the cells were incubated with SMase (Figure 9B), which is consistent with previous observations that SMase treatment increased cholesterol accessibility to PFO in fibroblasts (Das et al., 2013), increased MCD extraction of cholesterol from erythrocytes (Besenicar et al., 1778), and increased PM to ER trafficking of cholesterol in fibroblasts (Slotte and Bierman, 1988; Subbaiah et al., 2003; Ohvo et al., 1997).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B and supported by multiple citations.

claim: SMase treatment increased cholesterol accessibility to PFO in fibroblasts.
source: Increased fALOD4 binding was also seen after the cells were incubated with SMase (Figure 9B), which is consistent with previous observations that SMase treatment increased cholesterol accessibility to PFO in fibroblasts (Das et al., 2013), increased MCD extraction of cholesterol from erythrocytes (Besenicar et al., 1778), and increased PM to ER trafficking of cholesterol in fibroblasts (Slotte and Bierman, 1988; Subbaiah et al., 2003; Ohvo et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Das et al. (2013).

claim: SMase treatment increased MCD extraction of cholesterol from erythrocytes.
source: Increased fALOD4 binding was also seen after the cells were incubated with SMase (Figure 9B), which is consistent with previous observations that SMase treatment increased cholesterol accessibility to PFO in fibroblasts (Das et al., 2013), increased MCD extraction of cholesterol from erythrocytes (Besenicar et al., 1778), and increased PM to ER trafficking of cholesterol in fibroblasts (Slotte and Bierman, 1988; Subbaiah et al., 2003; Ohvo et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Besenicar et al. (1778).

claim: SMase treatment increased PM to ER trafficking of cholesterol in fibroblasts.
source: Increased fALOD4 binding was also seen after the cells were incubated with SMase (Figure 9B), which is consistent with previous observations that SMase treatment increased cholesterol accessibility to PFO in fibroblasts (Das et al., 2013), increased MCD extraction of cholesterol from erythrocytes (Besenicar et al., 1778), and increased PM to ER trafficking of cholesterol in fibroblasts (Slotte and Bierman, 1988; Subbaiah et al., 2003; Ohvo et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Slotte and Bierman (1988), Subbaiah et al. (2003), and Ohvo et al. (1997).

claim: The median fALOD4 binding was higher in Blacks than in Hispanics in the Dallas Biobank cohort.
source: The demographics and the distribution of fALOD4 binding in these individuals are shown in Table 4; the median fALOD4 binding was higher in Blacks than in Hispanics, which is similar to what we had seen in the other cohort (Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Table 4.

claim: LPE, SM, and phosphatidic acid levels were associated with differences in fALOD4 binding in a multivariable model adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, and plasma TG levels.
source: Differences in levels of several of the RBC lipids were observed between Blacks and Hispanics, however in a multivariable models adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, and plasma TG levels, only differences in lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LPE), SM, and phosphatidic acid levels were associated with differences in fALOD4 binding.
evidence: This is shown in Table 5.

claim: LPE accounted for 8.55% of variation in fALOD4 binding.
source: Individually, these lipids accounted for 8.55% (LPE), 0.01% (SM), and 3.62% (phosphatidic acid) of variation in fALOD4 binding, respectively (Table 5).
evidence: This is shown in Table 5.

claim: SM accounted for 0.01% of variation in fALOD4 binding.
source: Individually, these lipids accounted for 8.55% (LPE), 0.01% (SM), and 3.62% (phosphatidic acid) of variation in fALOD4 binding, respectively (Table 5).
evidence: This is shown in Table 5.

claim: Phosphatidic acid accounted for 3.62% of variation in fALOD4 binding.
source: Individually, these lipids accounted for 8.55% (LPE), 0.01% (SM), and 3.62% (phosphatidic acid) of variation in fALOD4 binding, respectively (Table 5).
evidence: This is shown in Table 5.

claim: RBC lipids accounted for 17.6% of the inter-individual variation in fALOD4 binding in a model adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity and plasma TG levels.
source: In this model the RBC lipids accounted for 17.6% of the inter-individual variation in fALOD4 binding (the R2 values are not additive because of the correlations among the RBC lipids).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis shown in Table 5.

claim: fALOD4 binding was significantly higher in RBCs from dialysis patients than in ethnically-matched controls, irrespective of ethnicity.
source: fALOD4 binding was significantly higher in RBCs from dialysis patients that in ethnically-matched controls, irrespective of ethnicity (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10A.

claim: fALOD4 binding was similar in paired samples obtained before and after a single dialysis treatment.
source: In eight individuals, fALOD4 binding was measured in RBCs prepared from blood samples obtained before and after a single dialysis treatment. fALOD4 binding was similar in the paired samples (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The increase in fALOD4 binding observed in dialysis patients was not an acute result of dialysis per se.
source: Therefore, the increase in fALOD4 binding observed in dialysis patients was not an acute result of dialysis per se.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 10B showing no change before and after dialysis.

claim: The amount of accessible cholesterol in RBC membranes is stable within an individual but varies >10 fold among individuals.
source: The major finding of the study is that the amount of accessible cholesterol in RBC membranes is stable within an individual but varies >10 fold among individuals.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The high degree of inter-individual variation in accessible cholesterol was unrelated to total cholesterol content of the RBC membrane.
source: The high degree of inter-individual variation was unrelated to total cholesterol content of the RBC membrane and modestly affected by pronase-sensitive changes in protein content of the RBC membrane.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The high degree of inter-individual variation in accessible cholesterol was modestly affected by pronase-sensitive changes in protein content of the RBC membrane.
source: The high degree of inter-individual variation was unrelated to total cholesterol content of the RBC membrane and modestly affected by pronase-sensitive changes in protein content of the RBC membrane.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8A.

claim: Differences in RBC phospholipid composition accounted for 17.6% of the inter-individual variability in accessible cholesterol.
source: Differences in RBC phospholipid composition of the RBC membrane accounted for 17.6% of the inter-individual variability (Table 5).
evidence: This is shown in Table 5.

claim: Cholesterol accessibility in RBCs varied significantly between ethnic groups.
source: Cholesterol accessibility in RBCs varied significantly between ethnic groups and correlated indirectly with plasma levels of TG (Figure 7), but not with the morphology or hemoglobin content of the RBCs (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and Table 2.

claim: Cholesterol accessibility correlated indirectly with plasma levels of TG.
source: Cholesterol accessibility in RBCs varied significantly between ethnic groups and correlated indirectly with plasma levels of TG (Figure 7), but not with the morphology or hemoglobin content of the RBCs (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cholesterol accessibility did not correlate with the morphology or hemoglobin content of the RBCs.
source: Cholesterol accessibility in RBCs varied significantly between ethnic groups and correlated indirectly with plasma levels of TG (Figure 7), but not with the morphology or hemoglobin content of the RBCs (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: The level of accessible cholesterol in RBCs in the population varies significantly among individuals in a stable fashion.
source: Thus, we have shown that the level of accessible cholesterol in RBCs in the population varies significantly among individuals in a stable fashion and we have identified several factors, both intrinsic and extrinsic to the RBC membrane, that contribute to the variation in RBC cholesterol accessibility.
evidence: This is supported by data throughout the Results section.

claim: Among individuals, relative fALOD4 binding to RBCs did not correlate with the total cholesterol content of the RBC membranes.
source: Among individuals, relative fALOD4 binding to RBCs did not correlate with the total cholesterol content of the RBC membranes (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The cholesterol in the RBC membrane that is accessible to fALOD4 represents a distinct pool (or state) of cholesterol.
source: Thus, the cholesterol in the RBC membrane that is accessible to fALOD4 represents a distinct pool (or state) of cholesterol, which is not reflected by direct assays of RBC cholesterol mass.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between cholesterol content and fALOD4 binding.

claim: The striking reproducibility of relative fALOD4 binding to RBCs within a given individual indicates that the factors that govern RBC cholesterol accessibility must be relatively stable.
source: The striking reproducibility of relative fALOD4 binding to RBCs within a given individual (Figure 3) indicates that the factors that govern RBC cholesterol accessibility must be relatively stable.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 3B.

claim: The lack of a relationship between cholesterol content and cholesterol accessibility in RBCs is similar to what has been observed among membranes from different organelles in mammalian cells.
source: The lack of a relationship between cholesterol content and cholesterol accessibility in RBCs is similar to what has been observed among membranes from different organelles in mammalian cells, For example, plasma membranes (PMs) have a cholesterol content of ~40 mole%, whereas the cholesterol content of the membranes from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is only ~5 mole% (Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sokolov and Radhakrishnan (2010).

claim: Plasma membranes have a cholesterol content of ~40 mole%.
source: For example, plasma membranes (PMs) have a cholesterol content of ~40 mole%, whereas the cholesterol content of the membranes from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is only ~5 mole% (Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sokolov and Radhakrishnan (2010).

claim: The cholesterol content of the membranes from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is only ~5 mole%.
source: For example, plasma membranes (PMs) have a cholesterol content of ~40 mole%, whereas the cholesterol content of the membranes from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is only ~5 mole% (Sokolov and Radhakrishnan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sokolov and Radhakrishnan (2010).

claim: Despite wide differences in cholesterol content, the chemical activity of cholesterol in PM and ER membranes may be similar.
source: Despite this wide difference in cholesterol content, the chemical activity of cholesterol in these two membranes may be similar (Radhakrishnan and McConnell, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Radhakrishnan and McConnell (2000).

claim: PM phospholipids interact more strongly with cholesterol than ER phospholipids.
source: This equivalence could be achieved if PM phospholipids interact more strongly with cholesterol than ER phospholipids, a plausible possibility based on extensive fractionation analysis of PM and ER lipids (Colbeau et al., 1971; Comte et al., 1976; Schroeder et al., 1976) and biophysical studies of the varying affinity of cholesterol for different phospholipids (McConnell and Radhakrishnan, 2003; Wattenberg and Silbert, 1983; Finean, 1953).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Fluctuations in membrane composition lead to changes in the chemical activity of cholesterol and could result in cholesterol transport between membranes.
source: Fluctuations in membrane composition lead to changes in the chemical activity of cholesterol and could result in cholesterol transport between membranes, either internally or externally.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference based on biophysical principles.

claim: In the case of the RBC, changes in cholesterol activity in the plasma membrane must equilibrate with cholesterol in lipoproteins, other plasma proteins, or with other cells.
source: In the case of the RBC, which has no internal organelle membranes, changes in cholesterol activity in the plasma membrane must equilibrate with cholesterol in lipoproteins, other plasma proteins, or with other cells, such as circulating leukocytes or endothelial cells (Lange and Steck, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Lange and Steck (2016).

claim: Treatment of RBCs with either PLA2 or SMase increased cholesterol accessibility.
source: We found that treatment of RBCs with either PLA2 or SMase increased cholesterol accessibility (Figure 9), a finding that is consistent with prior studies (Subbaiah et al., 2003; Slotte et al., 1989).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9 and supported by citations.

claim: Non-cholesterol lipids contributed significantly to inter-individual differences in cholesterol accessibility.
source: Non-cholesterol lipids contributed significantly to inter-individual differences in cholesterol accessibility (Table 4), but identifying exactly which lipid species contributed to the observed variation in cholesterol accessibility was not straightforward.
evidence: This is shown in Table 4 and Table 5.

claim: The complex population of phospholipids in the RBC membrane and the high degree of correlation between different phospholipid classes confounded the analysis.
source: The complex population of phospholipids in the RBC membrane and the high degree of correlation between different phospholipid classes confounded the analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the analytical challenges in interpreting the data.

claim: It is possible that differences in phospholipid composition alter the distribution of cholesterol between the two leaflets of the RBC membrane.
source: It is also possible that differences in phospholipid composition alter the distribution of cholesterol between the two leaflets of the RBC membrane.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: At cholesterol concentrations below the inflection point, the capacity of the membrane to incorporate cholesterol into complexes with phospholipids is high and the propensity for cholesterol to leave the membrane is low.
source: At cholesterol concentrations below the inflection point, the capacity of the membrane to incorporate cholesterol into complexes with phospholipids is high and the propensity for cholesterol to leave the membrane is low, therefore cholesterol will tend to accumulate in the RBC.
evidence: This is an inference based on biophysical principles of cholesterol-phospholipid interactions.

claim: At cholesterol concentrations above the inflection point, the capacity of the membrane to accommodate additional cholesterol in complexes with phospholipids is low, and cholesterol is poised to leave the RBC membrane when suitable acceptors become available.
source: At cholesterol concentrations above the inflection point, the capacity of the membrane to accommodate additional cholesterol in complexes with phospholipids is low, and cholesterol is poised to leave the RBC membrane when suitable acceptors become available.
evidence: This is an inference based on biophysical principles of cholesterol-phospholipid interactions.

claim: The cholesterol content of the RBC membranes is maintained close to equilibrium with respect to cholesterol exchange.
source: Thus, the cholesterol content of the RBC membranes is maintained close to equilibrium with respect to cholesterol exchange.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RBC cholesterol is near the threshold for accessibility.

claim: Depletion of membrane proteins by pronase digestion had only a modest effect on fALOD4 binding.
source: However, depletion of membrane proteins by pronase digestion had only a modest effect on fALOD4 binding (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: No association was found between ABO blood groups and fALOD4 binding.
source: No association was found between ABO blood groups and fALOD4 binding (Figure 8B, upper panel), but fALOD4 binding was reproducibly lower in those who were negative for the Rh antigen, a transmembrane protein of unknown function (Huang et al., 2000) (Figure 8B, lower panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B upper panel.

claim: fALOD4 binding was reproducibly lower in those who were negative for the Rh antigen.
source: No association was found between ABO blood groups and fALOD4 binding (Figure 8B, upper panel), but fALOD4 binding was reproducibly lower in those who were negative for the Rh antigen, a transmembrane protein of unknown function (Huang et al., 2000) (Figure 8B, lower panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B lower panel.

claim: Rh antigen is a transmembrane protein of unknown function.
source: No association was found between ABO blood groups and fALOD4 binding (Figure 8B, upper panel), but fALOD4 binding was reproducibly lower in those who were negative for the Rh antigen, a transmembrane protein of unknown function (Huang et al., 2000) (Figure 8B, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al. (2000).

claim: The effect of the Rh antigen on fALOD4 binding may be direct or indirect.
source: The effect of the Rh antigen on fALOD4 binding may be direct or indirect.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Rh antigen may compete with or directly inhibit fALOD4 binding.
source: Rh antigen may compete with or directly inhibit fALOD4 binding.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Rh antigen may alter the cholesterol accessibility in the RBC membrane.
source: Alternatively, the antigen may alter the cholesterol accessibility in the RBC membrane.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Factors that are extrinsic to the RBC were found to be associated with differences in RBC cholesterol accessibility.
source: Factors that are extrinsic to the RBC were also found to be associated with differences in RBC cholesterol accessibility.
evidence: This is supported by data showing associations with plasma TG levels.

claim: Lipoprotein lipids accounted for 5.4% of the variation in fALOD4 binding in a multivariate model that included gender and race.
source: Lipoprotein lipids accounted for 5.4% of the variation in fALOD4 binding in a multivariate model that included gender and race (Table 2).
evidence: This is calculated from Table 2 (TG 3.99% + total cholesterol 1.45%).

claim: Plasma levels of TG and RBC cholesterol accessibility were inversely correlated.
source: Plasma levels of TG and RBC cholesterol accessibility were inversely correlated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 and Table 2.

claim: The inverse correlation between plasma TG and RBC cholesterol accessibility may be a direct result of movement of accessible cholesterol from RBCs to very low density lipoproteins (VLDL).
source: This correlation may be a direct result of movement of accessible cholesterol from RBCs to very low density lipoproteins (VLDL) (Chung et al., 1986).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Chung et al. (1986).

claim: It is possible that circulating lipoproteins influence RBC cholesterol accessibility by transferring phospholipids to (or from) the RBC membrane.
source: It is also possible that circulating lipoproteins influence RBC cholesterol accessibility by transferring phospholipids to (or from) the RBC membrane (Reed, 1968).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Reed (1968).

claim: It is possible that ABCA1 transfers cholesterol directly from cells to RBCs.
source: It is possible that ABCA1 transfers cholesterol directly from cells to RBCs, and thus contributes to the flux of cholesterol from extrahepatic tissues to the liver (Figure 1).
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: RBCs do not have access to peripheral tissues unless there is loss of vascular integrity.
source: RBCs do not have access to peripheral tissues unless there is loss of vascular integrity, but they can interact indirectly with peripheral tissues through cells, such as macrophages, and lipoproteins that enter the tissues and return to the circulation.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of vascular anatomy and physiology.

claim: RBCs can interact indirectly with peripheral tissues through cells, such as macrophages, and lipoproteins that enter the tissues and return to the circulation.
source: RBCs do not have access to peripheral tissues unless there is loss of vascular integrity, but they can interact indirectly with peripheral tissues through cells, such as macrophages, and lipoproteins that enter the tissues and return to the circulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the circulation of cells and lipoproteins.

claim: RBCs have been shown to be excellent acceptors of free cholesterol from macrophages.
source: RBCs have been shown to be excellent acceptors of free cholesterol from macrophages (Ho et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ho et al. (1980).

claim: Brown and Goldstein found that RBCs were 6-fold more potent than whole serum as cholesterol acceptors from macrophages.
source: Brown and Goldstein found that RBCs were 6-fold more potent than whole serum as cholesterol acceptors from macrophages (Ho et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ho et al. (1980).

claim: Lipoprotein-depleted plasma is as efficient an acceptor as whole serum or plasma from cholesterol-loaded macrophages.
source: Lipoprotein-depleted plasma is as efficient an acceptor as whole serum or plasma from cholesterol-loaded macrophages (Ho et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ho et al. (1980).

claim: It is possible that blood components other than lipoproteins contribute to differences in cholesterol accessibility of the RBC membrane.
source: Although here we focused on the relationship between RBC accessible cholesterol and lipoprotein levels, it is also possible that blood components other than lipoproteins contribute to differences in cholesterol accessibility of the RBC membrane (Ho et al., 1980).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Ho et al. (1980).

claim: RBCs may exchange cholesterol with endothelial cells, thus indirectly transporting cholesterol from the tissues.
source: RBCs may also exchange cholesterol with endothelial cells, thus indirectly transporting cholesterol from the tissues.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: It is unlikely that RBCs deliver cholesterol directly to hepatocytes since they are too large to enter the space of Disse.
source: It is unlikely that RBCs deliver cholesterol directly to hepatocytes since they are too large to enter the space of Disse.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: Significant and systematic differences in RBC cholesterol activity were found among individuals of European, African, and Hispanic descent.
source: Significant and systematic differences in RBC cholesterol activity were found among individuals of European, African, and Hispanic descent.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 and Table 2.

claim: The increased RBC accessibility in Blacks was not fully explained by the measured differences in RBC lipid composition or by the plasma lipoprotein levels.
source: The increased RBC accessibility in Blacks was not fully explained by the measured differences in RBC lipid composition or by the plasma lipoprotein levels.
evidence: This is shown in Table 5 where ethnicity remains significant after adjustment.

claim: In linear regression analysis adjusted for RBC lipids and plasma lipoproteins, the proportion of variability in fALOD4 binding explained by ethnicity was reduced from 32% to 22.4%, but remained highly statistically significant.
source: In linear regression analysis, adjusted for these factors, the proportion of variability in fALOD4 binding explained by ethnicity was reduced from 32% to 22.4%, but remained highly statistically significant (Table 5).
evidence: This is shown in Table 5.

claim: Dietary differences between the ethnic groups may contribute to differences in RBC cholesterol accessibility.
source: Dietary differences between the ethnic groups may also contribute to differences in RBC cholesterol accessibility.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible contributing factor.

claim: Interethnic differences in cholesterol accessibility may be the consequence(s) of historic differences in selective pressure among the three ethnic groups.
source: Interethnic differences in cholesterol accessibility may be the consequence(s) of historic differences in selective pressure among the three ethnic groups.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: RBCs with higher fALOD4 binding would be anticipated to be more susceptible to microorganisms that produce cholesterol-binding toxins.
source: RBCs with higher fALOD4 binding would be anticipated to be more susceptible to microorganisms that produce cholesterol-binding toxins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of action of cholesterol-binding toxins.

claim: ALO is a member of the cholesterol-dependent cytolysin family, which is a family of pore-forming toxins produced by a myriad of different gram positive bacteria.
source: ALO, produced by Bacillus Anthracis, is a member of the cholesterol-dependent cytolysin family, which is a family of pore-forming toxins produced by a myriad of different gram positive bacteria, including species of Streptococcus, Listeria and Clostridium (Palmer, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Palmer (2001).

claim: Individuals with lower fALOD4 binding may be less susceptible to the hemolytic effects of cholesterol-binding toxins, thus providing them with a survival advantage.
source: Perhaps individuals with lower fALOD4 binding are less susceptible to the hemolytic effects of these toxins, thus providing them with a survival advantage.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary selection.

claim: Genetic and pharmacological studies have provided compelling evidence that increased circulating levels of HDL-cholesterol do not confer protection against coronary heart disease.
source: Genetic and pharmacological studies have provided compelling evidence that increased circulating levels of HDL-cholesterol, widely viewed as the vehicle for reverse cholesterol transport, do not confer protection against coronary heart disease (Siddiqi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Siddiqi et al. (2015).

claim: RBCs may be a conduit for transporting cholesterol from peripheral tissues to the liver.
source: RBCs may be a conduit for transporting cholesterol from peripheral tissues to the liver.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Mice made anemic had reduced fecal excretion of cholesterol from macrophages.
source: Mice made anemic had reduced fecal excretion of cholesterol from macrophages (Hung et al., 2012), and anemia has been shown to be associated with increased coronary artery disease (Hazard Ratio of 1.41 over 6 years) (Sarnak et al., 2002).

claim: Anemia has been shown to be associated with increased coronary artery disease (Hazard Ratio of 1.41 over 6 years).
source: Mice made anemic had reduced fecal excretion of cholesterol from macrophages (Hung et al., 2012), and anemia has been shown to be associated with increased coronary artery disease (Hazard Ratio of 1.41 over 6 years) (Sarnak et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sarnak et al. (2002).

claim: Patients with chronic renal failure on dialysis have a dramatically increased risk of atherosclerosis that is not explained by known risk factors.
source: To determine if RBC cholesterol accessibility provides a clinically relevant biomarker, we measured cholesterol accessibility in patients with chronic renal failure on dialysis, who have a dramatically increased risk of atherosclerosis that is not explained by known risk factors (Levey et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levey et al. (1998).

claim: A systematic increase in cholesterol accessibility was found in RBCs in patients on dialysis when compared to healthy age- and race-matched controls.
source: We found a systematic increase in cholesterol accessibility in RBCs in patients on dialysis when compared to healthy age- and race-matched controls.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10A.
